1.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he also sent trees of cedar]

As the parallel text in 1 Samuel 5:11 indicates, here **a wall** represents the stone that these **craftsmen** would use to build a wall. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and craftsmen of stone]

2.note: The expression **had been lifted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that Yahweh had lifted his kingdom to above]

Here the author is speaking of David’s **kingdom** as if it had been an object that could have been **lifted** physically to **above** (that is, to a great height). If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that Yahweh had made his kingdom prosperous and strong]

4.note: The expression **the ones born** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the ones his wives bore]

8.note: The expression **has been anointed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Israelites had anointed David]
See how you translated the similar expression in 11:6. Alternate translation: [and all of the Philistines went]
In a context such as this, your language might say “came” instead of **went**. [and all of the Philistines came]

The author is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [the whole Philistine army]
See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of this use of the term **faces**. Alternate translation: [to oppose them]

10.note: The parallel text in 1 Samuel 5:19 indicates that at this time, David was in a lower elevation than the Philistines. To translate these expressions and the similar one in the next verse, see how you translated the similar expression in 11:6. Alternate translation: [Shall I go against the Philistines … Go] or [Shall I attack the Philistines … Attack them]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:20. Alternate translation: [And will you enable me to defeat them? … I will enable you to defeat them]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [I will give them into your hand, so go up]

11.note: The pronoun **they** refers to David and his soldiers, while the pronoun **them** refers to the Philistines. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And David and his soldiers went up to Baal Perazim, and David struck the Philistines there]
See how you translated the term “struck” in 1:46. Alternate translation: [and David defeated them]

The author is using one person who was involved in defeating the Philistines, **David**, to mean all of the people who were involved. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and David and his soldiers defeated them]

Here, **hand** represents the capability or power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God has enabled me to break through my enemies] or [God has given me the power to break through my enemies]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **breaking through of waters** (that is, a flood of waters breaking through a dam, its banks, or some other restriction) is powerful and overwhelming, so was Yahweh’s defeat of David’s enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as powerfully as a rushing flood]

Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people call]
The name **Baal Perazim** means “the Lord of Breakthroughs.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain this in the text of your translation or in a footnote.

12.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the Philistines who were fleeing from David’s army. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Philistines abandoned]

Burning the Philistines’ idols was a symbolic action that illustrated the character of David’s victory over the Philistines and their gods. The Philistines had brought these idols into battle with them in the hopes that the gods they represented would help them defeat David and the Israelites. Instead, the gods themselves were shown to be helpless. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and David commanded his soldiers to burn their idols to show how weak and helpless the Philistine gods were compared to Yahweh]

The expression **were born** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and his soldiers burned them with fire]

It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [and his soldiers burned them up]

13.note: The author is using **added again** as a common expression of his culture to mean that someone did something for a further time. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the Philistines once again came] or [And the Philistines invaded again]

By **the valley**, the author means the Valley of the Raphaites, as in verse 9. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the Valley of the Raphaites]

14.note: While David would have had to move to a higher elevation in order to engage the Philistines, in this context, by telling him not to **go up**, Yahweh means that he should not make a direct, frontal attack. If this phrase would not have that meaning in your language in this context, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Do not make a frontal attack against them]

15.note: Here, **face** represents what is in front of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in advance of you]
See how you translated the similar expression in verse 11. Alternate translation: [to defeat]

Here, **camp** represents the army that has camped in a place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the army of the Philistines]

16.note: See how you translated the similar expressions in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [And he defeated the Philistine army]

17.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 5:24. Alternate translation: [And the reputation of David went out into all of the lands]

The author is speaking of David’s **name** or reputation as if it had been a living thing that could have gone out from Israel to the surrounding lands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And people in all of the lands heard of the reputation of David]

The author is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [into the surrounding lands]

The author is speaking as if the **fear** of David had been an object that Yahweh could have **put** **on** all of the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh made all of the nations afraid of him] or [and Yahweh made all of the nations respect him]
